title: Dependency Inversion Violation (High-Level Policy depending on Concrete Plugin)
pattern: A stable module containing core business logic or high-level policy directly references or imports concrete, volatile implementation details such as low-level frameworks, specific database clients, or physical device adapters.
why_bad: High-level policies are the most stable and high-value parts of the application. Allowing details to depend on policies keeps policies isolated. Reversing this direction forces re-compilation or breaks business policies whenever low-level machinery (e.g. database client upgrade) changes.
detection: Import declarations (`use`, `import`) referencing external technical dependency crates (such as PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis, AWS SDK) inside directories designated as core business domain modules.
counterexample: Adapter modules or system entry points explicitly designed to orchestrate and wire dependencies.
source: Robert C. Martin, *Clean Architecture* (2017), Chapter 14, "Component Coupling: The Dependency Inversion Principle", p. 263, 265.
